As we learn GitHub, staging, committing, and pushing everything is often a good habit because it keeps the local project and the GitHub repository synchronized.

title: More GitHub + Intro to Packages
text:
Out of sync
When you are out of sync, you can create something called a merge conflict. These are less common when you are the only one working on the project, but it can happen!
A merge conflict happens when Git tries to combine changes from two versions of a file that contain conflicting edits.
What does this look like?

Not staging all changed files → repositories may become out of sync.
Conflicting changes to the same parts of a file → potentially a merge conflict.

set.seed(3)

  colors = c("blue"),

This code is picking 10 random numbers, and plotting their path with a blue line as it approaches 1, following the rules of the conjecture.
part b

The canvas_collatz() function uses a random process. The argument n = 10 is giving us 10 random numbers. Each time we run the code, a new random process takes place, giving us 10 new random numbers and thus a new picture.
This might be troublesome because the picture will change every time we Render are document. This means that it will be impossible to describe the picture in our .qmd!
The set.seed() function ensures that the random state is fixed every time some code is run. This helps statisticians with reproducibility in simulation studies. The process of picking the numbers in the canvas_collatz() is still random, but those 10 random numbers are now fixed with set.seed().

text:
Motivation
For motivation, we are going to use the World Phones data set. Suppose I want to calculate the mean phone length for each year and country combination. Can I do that?
No… or at least not easily using the tidyverse.

WorldPhones

1956  60423  29990 4708   2568    2366   1411      733
1957  64721  32510 5230   2695    2526   1546      773
1958  68484  35218 6662   2845    2691   1663      836
1959  71799  37598 6856   3000    2868   1769      911
1960  76036  40341 8220   3145    3054   1905     1008
1961  79831  43173 9053   3338    3224   2005     1076


Are these data considered wide or long? What did we learn from this exercise?
This is a wide data set! Multiple values of a variable (phone count) are stored in separate columns (region) rather than in separate rows. We only have one row per year for each region!
This makes the data harder to work with.

x <- tibble(
  state = rep(c("MT", "NC" , "SC"),2),

Pivot these data so that the data are wide. i.e. Each state should be it’s own unique observation (row). Save this new data set as y.

y <- x |>

Data Format (Wide vs Long)
Wide data contains values that do not repeat in the first column (short-cut definition for most situations)
Wide data are data in which multiple values of a variable (often measurements taken under different conditions or at different times) are stored in separate columns rather than in separate rows.
Long data contains values that do repeat in the first column (short-cut definition for most situations)
Long data are data in which multiple measurements of the same observational unit are stored in separate rows, with one or more columns identifying the measurement or condition associated with each row.
